content: Preterm infants are typically cared for in incubators, but cot-nursing has been proposed as an alternative. While cot-nursing may offer certain advantages, such as easier access to the infant, it also carries potential risks, including an increased likelihood of nosocomial infections due to more frequent handling. The objective of this study was to evaluate the effects of cot-nursing compared to incubator care on two primary outcomes: temperature regulation and weight gain in preterm infants. The researchers employed the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's standard search strategy. This involved searching multiple electronic databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, the Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials, MEDLINE, CINAHL, and EMBASE, as well as reviewing previous studies and cross-references. The search covered literature up to November 2009. The inclusion criteria for the analysis were randomized or quasi-randomized trials that compared preterm infants cared for in standard newborn cots to those managed in conventional air-heated incubators. The authors independently evaluated the quality of the trials and extracted data related to the primary outcomes of temperature control and weight gain. A meta-analysis was performed using a fixed-effect model. Out of 11 potential studies identified, five trials involving a total of 247 infants met the inclusion criteria and were included in the review. The findings showed no significant difference in mean body temperature between cot-nursing and incubator care (mean difference [MD] 0.02°C; 95% confidence interval [CI] -0.02 to 0.07, based on four trials). However, one trial reported that episodes of hyperthermia were statistically more frequent in the cot-nursing group (relative risk [RR] 1.48; 95% CI 1.04 to 2.09). There were no statistically significant differences in weight gain between the two groups. In the cot-nursing group, fewer infants were breastfed at the time of hospital discharge (typical RR 0.74; 95% CI 0.48 to 1.14, based on three trials involving 150 infants). Additionally, fewer infants in the cot-nursing group died before hospital discharge (typical RR 0.59; 95% CI 0.28 to 1.25, based on four trials involving 235 infants), but these findings were not statistically significant. When cot-nursing with a heated water-filled mattress was compared to incubator care, the results were similar in terms of temperature control and weight gain. However, in one trial involving 38 infants, cot-nursing in a nursery warmed by space heating was associated with significantly lower weight gain during the first week (MD -5.90 g/kg/day; 95% CI -11.13 to -0.67). No significant differences in weight gain were observed during the second and third weeks. The authors concluded that cot-nursing using a heated water-filled mattress has comparable effects to incubator care in terms of temperature regulation and weight gain. However, further randomized controlled trials are needed to investigate important clinical outcomes, particularly in developing countries where differences in these outcomes may be more pronounced. Due to the limited data available, cot-nursing in a space-heated room is not currently recommended as a standard practice.
